Kitchen SOP Guide

Five core standards that keep every kitchen safe, clean and consistent: quality, hygiene, consistency and safety.

By Nigel A. Thomas, Hospitality Executive · Updated October 2026

Every kitchen runs on habits. The question is whether those habits are written down, taught and checked, or whether they live only in the heads of the senior cooks. A Standard Operating Procedure, or SOP, is the document that turns good habits into a shared standard: a clear, step-by-step instruction for how a task must be done, by whom, how often and what happens when it goes wrong. Kitchens with strong SOPs serve safer food, waste less, train faster and stay calm under pressure, because everyone already knows what “right” looks like.

This guide goes with the Kitchen SOP poster below. The poster distils the standard into five core areas: personal hygiene, food safety, storage and labeling, cleaning and sanitation, and kitchen discipline, all held together by four values: quality, hygiene, consistency and safety. In this article I expand every area into practical, usable detail, show how to write and roll out SOPs that people actually follow, and explain how to check that they are working. After more than thirty years in hospitality, on ships, in hotels and in restaurants across India, the Middle East and the USA, I can say that the kitchens that struggle are rarely short of knowledge. They are short of a system.

What Is a Kitchen SOP and Why Does It Matter?

An SOP is a written procedure that describes how a routine task is performed in a consistent, safe and efficient way. In a kitchen that can mean anything from how to wash hands properly to how to receive a delivery, cool a large batch of stock or break down a station at the end of service. SOPs sit beneath your food safety plan. If the plan tells you what hazards must be controlled, the SOPs tell the team how to control them every single day.

The benefits are practical and measurable:

  • Food safety: written, repeatable controls reduce the risk of contamination, temperature abuse and foodborne illness.
  • Consistency: the same dish tastes and looks the same whoever is on the pass, which is what guests remember.
  • Faster training: new starters learn from a clear standard instead of copying whatever the person next to them does.
  • Less waste and lower cost: portion control, correct storage and rotation protect margins.
  • Compliance and audit readiness: inspectors and auditors look for documented procedures and evidence that they are followed.
  • Accountability: when a standard is written down, it is fair and clear when it is not met.

The Anatomy of a Good SOP

A good SOP is short, specific and easy to follow in the middle of a busy shift. It is not a policy essay. Whatever format you choose, every SOP should answer the same questions:

  • Purpose: why does this procedure exist?
  • Scope: where and for whom does it apply?
  • Responsibility: who performs it, and who checks it?
  • Steps: numbered actions in the order they are done, using plain verbs.
  • Critical limits: the measurable standards, such as temperatures, times and concentrations.
  • Records: which log or checklist is completed, and where it is kept.
  • Corrective action: what to do if the standard is not met.
  • Review date: when the SOP will next be reviewed and who owns it.

Keep each SOP to a page where possible, write it in the language your team actually speaks, and use photographs or simple diagrams to show correct practice. A procedure that cannot be understood at a glance will not be used.

Standard 1: Personal Hygiene

People are the single biggest source of contamination in a kitchen, and personal hygiene is therefore the first line of defence. The poster reduces it to three habits: a clean uniform, handwashing and hair covered. Each one deserves a clear standard.

Clean uniform

Staff should arrive in a clean uniform and change if it becomes soiled. Uniforms should be worn in the kitchen only, and street clothes, bags and personal items kept in lockers away from food areas. Aprons should come off before staff visit the toilet or leave the production area, and a fresh apron should be used when moving from raw to ready-to-eat tasks.

Handwashing

Handwashing is the most effective and least expensive control you have. The SOP should state exactly when hands must be washed: on entering the kitchen, after using the toilet, after handling raw meat, poultry, fish or eggs, after touching the face, hair, phone or waste, after cleaning, after breaks, and before putting on fresh gloves. The method should be just as clear: wet hands with warm water, apply soap, scrub all surfaces including thumbs, fingertips and between the fingers for around 20 seconds in total, rinse, and dry with a single-use towel. Handwash basins must be dedicated, stocked with soap and towels, and never used for washing food or equipment.

Hair covered and other rules

Hair must be tied back and covered with a hat or net, and beards covered where required. Nails should be short and clean, jewellery limited to a plain band, and cuts covered with a bright, waterproof dressing. Staff who are unwell, particularly with vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice or infected wounds, must report it and must not handle food until your procedure and local regulations allow, which is often at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. A culture where people feel safe reporting illness is worth more than any poster.

Standard 2: Food Safety

The poster summarises food safety as three actions: prevent cross-contamination, use colour-coded boards and check temperatures. They map to the three biggest hazards in any kitchen: contamination, confusion between raw and cooked, and temperature abuse.

Prevent cross-contamination

Cross-contamination happens when bacteria, allergens or chemicals move from one food, surface or person to another. Prevent it by keeping raw and ready-to-eat food apart in storage, preparation and service, by using separate equipment for raw and cooked items, by washing hands between tasks, and by cleaning and sanitising surfaces between uses. Raw poultry, meat and fish must never touch or drip onto food that will not be cooked again. Allergens need the same discipline: dedicated utensils, clear labeling and strict handling for allergen-free orders.

Use colour-coded boards

Colour coding makes the right choice the easy choice. A common system uses red boards and knives for raw meat, blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat, green for salad and fruit, brown for root vegetables and white for bakery and dairy. Schemes differ between countries and companies, so the exact colours matter less than choosing one scheme, displaying it on the wall, buying matching equipment and enforcing it without exception. Replace boards that are deeply scored, because bacteria can hide in the grooves.

Check temperatures

Bacteria multiply fastest in the danger zone between about 5°C and 60°C. The SOP should set clear limits and make them measurable, using calibrated probe thermometers:

  • Chilled storage: 5°C or below. Frozen storage: minus 18°C or below.
  • Hot holding: 60°C or above (in the USA, 57°C or 135°F).
  • Cooking: poultry to a core temperature of 74°C, minced products to 71°C, and whole cuts of beef, lamb and pork to 63°C with a short rest.
  • Reheating: bring food to 74°C throughout, and do it once only.
  • Cooling: cool cooked food quickly, for example from 60°C to 21°C within two hours and to 5°C within a further four, using shallow containers and ice baths.

Record the readings. Our kitchen temperature log sheet and the kitchen equipment temperature guide give you ready-to-use references for what to measure and where.

Standard 3: Storage and Labeling

Good storage protects food safety, quality and profit at the same time. The poster lists four rules: FIFO, date labels, covered containers and correct storage.

  • FIFO (First In, First Out): new stock goes behind older stock, and older stock is used first. This prevents waste and makes sure nothing is forgotten at the back of the walk-in.
  • Date labels: every prepared or opened item carries a label showing what it is, when it was prepared or opened, and its use-by date. The shelf life is set by your food safety plan, and anything out of date is discarded without discussion.
  • Covered containers: food is stored in clean, food-grade, lidded containers or wrapped, which protects it from contamination, odours and drying out.
  • Correct storage: store ready-to-eat food above raw food, with raw poultry on the lowest shelf. Keep everything off the floor, and store chemicals well away from food, ideally below and in a separate area.

Receiving is where good storage begins. Check delivery temperatures, packaging, dates and condition before anything is signed for, and move chilled and frozen goods into storage promptly. Do not overload refrigerators, because air must circulate to keep every shelf at temperature. A weekly stock rotation check, with a manager’s signature, keeps the standard alive.

Standard 4: Cleaning and Sanitation

Cleaning removes visible dirt and grease. Sanitising reduces bacteria to a safe level. Both are needed, in that order, because sanitiser does not work properly on a dirty surface. The poster boils this standard down to clean as you go, sanitise workstations and keep floors dry.

Clean as you go

A kitchen that is cleaned only at the end of the night is a kitchen that is never really clean. Teach cooks to wipe, sweep and tidy as they work, to clear their station between tasks and to leave nothing for later. It also makes the closing clean faster and the working day safer.

Sanitise workstations

Work surfaces, boards, knives, probes and equipment that touch food must be cleaned and sanitised between tasks, particularly after raw food. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for dilution and contact time, and use test strips where the product requires them. Wiping cloths should be kept in sanitiser solution and changed often. Keep cleaning chemicals in labelled containers and never decant them into food or drink bottles.

Keep floors dry

Wet and greasy floors cause slips, which are among the most common kitchen injuries. Mop spills at once, put out wet-floor signs, use non-slip mats and footwear, and fix leaks and drainage problems rather than working around them. Beyond daily tasks, a written cleaning schedule assigns each area, item and frequency to a named person. The kitchen cleaning schedule template is a good starting point for building one.

Standard 5: Kitchen Discipline

Discipline is what makes the other four standards stick. The poster names three behaviours: follow recipes, control portions and report hazards. They look simple, and in a busy service they are the first to slip.

  • Follow recipes: standardised recipes with exact ingredients, quantities, methods and photographs protect quality and consistency. Changing a recipe on the fly confuses the team, upsets costing and can introduce allergens without anyone knowing.
  • Control portions: use scales, scoops, ladles and portion tools. Consistent portions protect food cost, guest satisfaction and fairness between tables, and they cut waste.
  • Report hazards: broken equipment, spills, near misses, pest sightings, faulty probes and unsafe practices should be reported immediately and without blame. A kitchen that hides its problems cannot fix them.

Discipline also covers the small professional habits: a mise en place completed before service, clear calls on the pass, knives stored and carried safely, phones kept out of the production area, and respect between the team. Leaders set the tone, because the standard a manager walks past is the standard they have accepted.

How to Write SOPs People Will Actually Follow

  • Start with the risk. Write SOPs first for the tasks that carry the most risk: handwashing, receiving, cooking and cooling, allergen handling, cleaning and sanitising, and illness reporting.
  • Involve the people who do the job. Cooks and stewards know where the real problems are, and they will own a procedure they helped write.
  • Use plain language and numbered steps. One action per step, starting with a verb.
  • Show it. Photographs and simple diagrams beat paragraphs. Post key SOPs at the point of use, such as the handwash sink or the cooling station.
  • Make the standard measurable. “Keep it cold” is vague. “Store at 5°C or below and record twice a day” can be checked.
  • Version and date them. Keep a controlled copy, remove outdated ones and record who approved each change.

A short example: the handwashing SOP

ElementStandard
PurposePrevent contamination of food by hands
WhoAll kitchen, stewarding and service staff entering the production area
WhenOn entry, after the toilet, after raw food, after waste, after touching face or phone, between tasks
MethodWet, soap, scrub for about 20 seconds, rinse, dry with a single-use towel
RecordsSupervisor spot checks logged each shift
If not followedRetrain on the spot, record it, and review if it repeats

Opening and Closing Checklists

Two of the most useful SOPs in any kitchen are the opening and closing checklists. They bookend the day, catch problems early and make sure that nothing important depends on someone’s memory.

  • Opening: check fridge and freezer temperatures and record them, inspect the previous day’s labels, confirm that handwash stations are stocked, check sanitiser strength, calibrate or check probe thermometers, confirm that equipment works, and brief the team on specials, allergens and any absences.
  • Closing: cool, label and store all prepared food, wrap and date everything, clean and sanitise all stations and equipment, empty and clean bins, sweep and mop floors, switch off equipment according to the procedure, lock chemicals away, and sign off the checklist before leaving.

A signature at the bottom of each checklist creates accountability. The next shift can see at once whether the kitchen was left in the right state, and a manager can spot patterns, such as a station that is always missed, before they become a problem.

Allergen Management as an SOP

Allergens deserve their own procedure because the consequences of a mistake can be severe. A sound allergen SOP identifies the major allergens in every recipe, keeps an up-to-date allergen matrix, and makes sure that every order with an allergy request is passed to the kitchen clearly and handled separately. Use clean utensils, boards and pans, wash hands and change gloves, label allergen-free items clearly during delivery to the table, and never guess. If staff are unsure, they must ask the chef or manager. Train service and kitchen teams together so that the guest hears a consistent, confident answer.

Training and Rolling Out Your SOPs

An SOP that sits in a folder protects nobody. Rollout is where most kitchens fail, so treat it as a project with a plan:

  • Induct every new starter on the core SOPs before they handle food, and sign off the training in their record.
  • Train on the floor, not only in a classroom: demonstrate, let the person practise, and then observe them doing it correctly.
  • Run short daily briefings that revisit one standard at a time, which keeps habits fresh without long meetings.
  • Use the poster as a visual anchor in the changing room, at the pass and at handwash stations.
  • Refresh regularly, especially after incidents, menu changes or new equipment.

Monitoring, Records and Corrective Action

Monitoring is how you prove that the standard is real. Every critical SOP needs a check, a record and a response. Daily logs for fridge and freezer temperatures, cooking and cooling records, cleaning sign-offs, delivery checks and calibration records give you evidence and early warnings. Supervisors should walk the kitchen with a simple checklist each shift, and managers should carry out a more detailed weekly audit.

When a check fails, the SOP should already tell the team what to do. A fridge reading above 5°C triggers a recheck, a decision on food safety, a call to maintenance and a note in the log. Corrective action should always include the cause: if the same problem keeps happening, the answer is to fix the system, not just to blame the individual. Common SOP Mistakes to Avoid

  • Writing long, legalistic documents that nobody reads.
  • Copying a template without adapting it to your kitchen, your menu and your equipment.
  • Failing to train, or training once and never again.
  • Having SOPs but no records, so nothing can be proven.
  • Never reviewing or updating them after changes.
  • Enforcing standards on junior staff but excusing senior ones.
  • Treating mistakes as blame events rather than learning events.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many SOPs does a kitchen need?

There is no fixed number. Start with the high-risk tasks and add more as needed. Many kitchens operate well with 15 to 30 short, focused SOPs that cover their key processes.

Who is responsible for SOPs?

The head chef or kitchen manager owns them, but every team member is responsible for following them. Someone should be named as the owner of each document.

How often should SOPs be reviewed?

At least once a year, and also whenever there is an incident, a change in menu, equipment or regulation, or an audit finding.

Do SOPs replace a HACCP plan?

No. A HACCP plan identifies the hazards and critical control points. SOPs are the practical instructions and records that make the plan work in daily operation. Follow the food safety regulations that apply in your country, such as FSSAI in India.

How do I get the team to follow them?

Involve them in writing the SOPs, train properly, make the standard easy to follow, check it consistently, and lead by example. People follow what is inspected and what their leaders do.

Final Thoughts

A great kitchen is not built on talent alone. It is built on standards that everyone understands and keeps: clean hands, safe temperatures, labeled and rotated stock, a tidy and sanitised workspace, and the discipline to follow the recipe and report a hazard. The Kitchen SOP poster captures those five areas on a single page, and the four values at its foot, quality, hygiene, consistency and safety, are the reason they matter.

Print the poster, put it where your team can see it, write your SOPs one process at a time, train until the habits are automatic and check until the standard becomes part of the culture.
